title: Tonkotsu Ramen
subtitle: Creamy pork bone broth with noodles and chashu pork
excerpt: A rich, milky pork bone broth made by boiling trotters and bones at a rolling boil for hours until the stock turns thick and white. Served with ramen noodles, sliced chashu pork, soft-boiled egg, and nori.

recipe.sourceNotes: Tonkotsu ramen originated in Fukuoka on the southern Japanese island of Kyushu and is one of the four major regional styles of Japanese ramen. The word tonkotsu means pork bone, and the style is defined by its opaque, milky-white broth produced by boiling pork bones at a high, rolling boil for a long time: typically 6 to 12 hours in restaurant kitchens, though 3 to 4 hours at home gives a good result. The emulsification of fat and collagen into the water is what creates the characteristic richness and opacity. Tonkotsu ramen became widely known outside Japan through the influence of Hakata-style ramen shops and was popularised internationally by the global expansion of Japanese ramen culture from the 1990s.

recipeTools.notes: A very large, heavy pot is needed for the long broth cook.

content.text: The key to a tonkotsu broth at home is maintaining a genuine rolling boil, not a gentle simmer. The vigorous boil emulsifies the fat and collagen into the water, turning the stock cloudy and thick. A timid simmer produces a thin, pale stock. The pork bones should be blanched first to remove blood and impurities. Chashu pork can be made the day before and refrigerated: it is much easier to slice thinly when cold.

items.preparation: 600g for chashu (skin-on); 400g off-cuts or extra belly for the broth

content.text: Make the broth: put the blanched, rinsed bones in a large pot with 3 litres of cold water, the garlic, ginger, and spring onions. Bring to a rapid boil and maintain a rolling boil for 3 to 4 hours, topping up with water as needed. The stock will turn opaque and white. Strain through a fine sieve. Season with salt.

Make the chashu: roll the pork belly tightly and tie with kitchen string. Sear all over in a hot pan. Add soy sauce, mirin, and sake. Cover and braise on the lowest heat for 1.5 hours, turning every 30 minutes, until very tender. Cool, then refrigerate. Slice thinly to serve.

Make the ramen eggs: boil the eggs for 6 minutes 30 seconds. Transfer to ice water, peel, then marinate in a mixture of 4 tablespoons soy sauce and 2 tablespoons mirin topped up with water to cover. Marinate for at least 2 hours.

To serve: cook the noodles according to the packet. Ladle the hot broth into bowls. Add noodles. Top with 2 to 3 slices of chashu, a halved ramen egg, and a sheet of nori. Drizzle with sesame oil. Serve immediately.
